GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__Oesophageal Manom:
Oesophageal manometry is a functional test that measures the pressure, strength and coordination of oesophageal contractions and the behaviour of the lower oesophageal sphincter (LOS) during swallowing. It is the gold-standard investigation for primary oesophageal motility disorders and is used to diagnose achalasia, characterise dysphagia when endoscopy is structurally normal, and map motility before anti-reflux surgery. High-resolution manometry (HRM) displays pressures as a colour topography plot interpreted using the Chicago Classification.

1Indication & principle

The test answers a functional question: is the muscle pump and its outlet valve working?

Non-obstructive dysphagia — difficulty swallowing when endoscopy (and often barium swallow) shows no stricture, ring or tumour.
Suspected motility disorder — especially achalasia, but also diffuse (distal) oesophageal spasm and ineffective motility.
Pre-operative work-up — mandatory before anti-reflux (fundoplication) surgery to exclude achalasia or a severe motility disorder that would contraindicate a wrap, and to site the pH probe accurately.

Principle: a fine pressure-sensing catheter passed transnasally records intraluminal pressure along the whole oesophagus. During standardised test swallows (typically 10 wet swallows of ~5 mL water) it captures the amplitude, velocity and coordination of the peristaltic wave and the resting tone and swallow-induced relaxation of the LOS.

2How it is performed
Preparation: nil by mouth for ~6 hours; stop drugs that alter motility where safe (nitrates, calcium-channel blockers, prokinetics, opioids).
Intubation: the catheter is passed transnasally into the stomach with the patient awake and seated, then withdrawn to straddle the LOS; local anaesthetic gel aids passage. No sedation is used as swallowing must be voluntary.
Protocol: a baseline resting period identifies LOS pressure, followed by a series of timed wet swallows spaced ~30 seconds apart to avoid deglutitive inhibition.
Output: HRM generates a spatiotemporal pressure plot; key metrics include the integrated relaxation pressure (IRP) of the LOS and the distal contractile integral (DCI) of the peristaltic wave.
3Interpretation

Patterns are matched to recognised motility diagnoses:

Absent peristalsis + failure of LOS relaxation (raised IRP) + raised LOS resting pressure→ACHALASIA
Premature, uncoordinated, simultaneous high-amplitude contractions with normal LOS relaxation→Diffuse (distal) oesophageal spasm
Weak or absent peristalsis + hypotensive LOS→Ineffective oesophageal motility (systemic sclerosis / scleroderma oesophagus)
Normal-amplitude, coordinated peristalsis with normal LOS relaxation→Excludes a primary motility disorder
🧪Achalasia
Non-relaxing hypertensive LOS + absent peristalsis; birds-beak on barium
⚡Distal spasm
Premature simultaneous contractions; corkscrew oesophagus on barium
🌀Scleroderma
Weak/absent peristalsis + patulous hypotensive LOS → severe reflux
📈IRP
Integrated relaxation pressure; raised = failure of LOS to relax (achalasia)
4Pitfalls, limitations & safety
Not a first-line test: upper GI endoscopy must precede manometry to exclude a mechanical or malignant cause.
Pseudoachalasia: a tumour at the gastro-oesophageal junction can mimic achalasia manometrically — suspect in older patients with short history and marked weight loss.
Technical limits: requires a cooperative, awake patient able to swallow to command; results affected by motility-altering drugs and by poor catheter positioning.
Contraindications: avoid in obstructing lesions, recent oesophageal perforation, or severe coagulopathy affecting nasal passage.
🚩 Endoscopy must be done FIRST to exclude malignancy or mechanical obstruction masquerading as achalasia (pseudoachalasia from a tumour at the gastro-oesophageal junction). New-onset dysphagia with weight loss is a red flag mandating urgent endoscopy before any functional test.
🎓 Achalasia = absent peristalsis + a non-relaxing hypertensive LOS on manometry; barium swallow shows the classic birds-beak tapering. Always endoscope first to exclude pseudoachalasia.
Achalasia confirmed — definitive treatment→pneumatic (balloon) dilatation, laparoscopic Heller myotomy (± partial fundoplication) or POEM (per-oral endoscopic myotomy); botulinum toxin injection is reserved for those unfit for definitive therapy. Achalasia ›
Distal oesophageal spasm (premature contractions; corkscrew on barium)→smooth-muscle relaxants — a calcium-channel blocker or nitrate — plus reassurance and treatment of any coexisting reflux.
Scleroderma oesophagus (absent contractility + hypotensive/patulous LOS)→aggressive high-dose PPI for the severe reflux this causes; the poor peristaltic reserve makes a fundoplication wrap high-risk, so it is generally avoided. Connective tissue disease › GORD ›
Which onward test?→structure/mucosa → endoscopy; reflux quantification → 24h pH/impedance; motility → manometry. Each answers a different question.
Hypercontractile “jackhammer” oesophagus→very high contractile vigour (DCI) with normal LOS relaxation; presents with chest pain/dysphagia.
🎓 Exam pearl. Work-up order: endoscopy first (exclude mechanical/malignant disease and pseudoachalasia), then a barium swallow (bird’s-beak = achalasia; corkscrew = spasm) as a complementary test — but manometry remains the gold standard for motility. Oesophageal cancer ›
GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__24h pH / Impedanc:
24-hour pH (and pH-impedance) monitoring is the reference-standard test for quantifying gastro-oesophageal reflux. A thin catheter with a pH electrode positioned ~5 cm above the lower oesophageal sphincter (LOS) records how long the distal oesophagus is exposed to acid over 24 hours; adding multichannel intraluminal impedance lets it detect non-acid and gas reflux and track bolus movement. It is used to prove or disprove GORD when the diagnosis is genuinely uncertain and, crucially, to decide whether a patient will benefit from anti-reflux surgery.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Endoscopy diagnoses reflux complications (oesophagitis, Barrett's) but is often normal in GORD. pH/impedance testing objectively quantifies reflux itself and links it to symptoms.

Diagnosis uncertain and endoscopy normal (non-erosive reflux disease).
PPI-refractory symptoms — is there ongoing reflux, or another cause?
Mandatory work-up before anti-reflux (fundoplication) surgery.
Atypical symptoms (chronic cough, chest pain, laryngitis) needing symptom–reflux correlation.

Principle: a distal pH electrode logs every drop below pH 4 (an acid reflux event); impedance measures changes in resistance between electrode pairs to detect any bolus — liquid, gas, acid or non-acid — and its direction of travel.

2HOW IT IS PERFORMED
A trans-nasal catheter is placed with the sensor 5 cm above the manometrically-located LOS (so oesophageal manometry is usually done first).
A wireless Bravo capsule can be clipped to the mucosa at endoscopy instead, allowing 48–96 h of catheter-free recording — better tolerated.
The patient keeps a diary, pressing event buttons for symptoms, meals and posture (upright/supine) over the study period.
Normal eating and activity are encouraged to reproduce everyday reflux.
3INTERPRETATION

The core metric is acid exposure time (AET) — the percentage of the study with pH < 4. The composite DeMeester score combines six parameters (a score >14.7 is abnormal). Symptom association is graded with the symptom index and symptom association probability.

AET (pH < 4) > 6% of study (4–6% is a borderline grey zone) / DeMeester > 14.7→Pathological acid reflux — GORD confirmed
Symptoms coincide with reflux events (positive symptom index ≥ 50%)→Symptoms are genuinely reflux-driven
Normal AET but symptoms tied to non-acid reflux on impedance→Non-acid / weakly-acidic (functional) reflux
Normal study but ongoing symptoms, no reflux correlation→Functional heartburn — not GORD
🧪Acid exposure time
% study pH < 4; > 6% is clearly pathological
📊DeMeester score
Composite acid index; > 14.7 abnormal
🔌Impedance
Detects non-acid & gas reflux, bolus direction
🔗Symptom index
Links each symptom to reflux events
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
Electrode misplacement or catheter migration distorts AET — correct positioning is essential.
Day-to-day reflux varies, so a single normal study does not fully exclude reflux if suspicion is high.
Nasal catheters are uncomfortable and may suppress normal eating, under-representing true reflux.
Bravo capsules can cause chest discomfort or, rarely, early detachment.
🚩 Always clarify the clinical question before the study. Testing OFF PPI (stopped ~7 days beforehand) confirms whether GORD exists; testing ON PPI assesses treatment failure and breakthrough reflux. A normal pH study in a symptomatic patient points AWAY from acid reflux and is a strong argument AGAINST anti-reflux surgery — operating on functional heartburn will not help and may harm.
🎓 Acid exposure time and DeMeester score quantify acid reflux; impedance adds non-acid and gas reflux plus symptom correlation. The combined result is what steers the key decision: whether fundoplication is likely to abolish the patient's symptoms.
Normal AET + symptoms NOT linked to reflux→functional heartburn: reassure and trial a neuromodulator (low-dose amitriptyline or an SSRI); do NOT escalate acid suppression or offer fundoplication.
Normal AET but symptoms reproducibly coincide with (physiological) reflux→positive symptom index (≥50%) / SAP (>95%) → reflux hypersensitivity, not GORD — neuromodulator ± targeted therapy rather than more acid suppression.
Confirmed pathological acid reflux — who does well from surgery?→good fundoplication-outcome predictors are pathological AET/DeMeester + positive symptom index + a prior response to PPI; reserve surgery for these (or patients wanting off lifelong PPI). GORD ›
Symptomatic non-acid reflux on PPI→volume-directed measures (alginate, weight loss, lifestyle); more acid suppression will not help, though selected refractory cases with a positive impedance–symptom link may still be surgical.
🎓 Exam pearl. A normal study is a positive result: it re-routes the patient away from surgery towards functional heartburn / reflux hypersensitivity (neuromodulators), not more PPI. Barrett’s ›
GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__Faecal Calprotect:
Faecal calprotectin is a stool test that measures a neutrophil-derived protein to detect inflammation in the gut. In a younger patient with chronic bowel symptoms and no alarm features, it is a NICE-endorsed triage test that helps distinguish inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) — Crohn's or ulcerative colitis — from irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), and so decides who genuinely needs a colonoscopy.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Calprotectin is a calcium- and zinc-binding protein that makes up the bulk of neutrophil cytosol. When neutrophils infiltrate an inflamed intestinal mucosa, they release calprotectin, which is stable in stool and resists degradation — making it a sensitive marker of active intestinal inflammation.

Use in adults with chronic (≥6 weeks) lower-GI symptoms where IBD is a possibility but cancer is not suspected.
Purpose: triage — separate organic inflammation (IBD) from a functional disorder (IBS) so colonoscopy is targeted, not universal.
IBS is functional, so calprotectin is typically normal; IBD involves mucosal inflammation, so it is typically raised.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED
A single random stool sample is collected by the patient and sent for laboratory ELISA quantification, reported in micrograms per gram (µg/g).
No dietary preparation or bowel prep is required, but the patient should ideally stop NSAIDs beforehand as these falsely elevate the result.
Avoid testing during an obvious acute gastroenteritis, as transient infection raises the level and confounds interpretation.
Borderline results are commonly rechecked on a repeat sample a few weeks later.
3INTERPRETATION
Normal <50 µg/g→Significant inflammation unlikely — supports IBS, colonoscopy can usually be avoided
Borderline ~50–150 µg/g→Indeterminate — repeat the test and correlate with the clinical picture
Raised >150–250 µg/g→Intestinal inflammation likely — refer for colonoscopy + mucosal biopsy to diagnose IBD
Rising level in known IBD→Suggests active disease or impending relapse — useful for monitoring and titrating therapy
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS

Calprotectin is highly sensitive but poorly specific — it flags inflammation of any cause, not IBD specifically. Know the common non-IBD causes of a raised result:

💊NSAIDs
Cause NSAID enteropathy and falsely elevate the level
🦠GI infection
Bacterial/viral gastroenteritis transiently raises it
🌾Coeliac disease
Mucosal inflammation can elevate the marker
⚠️Colorectal cancer
Malignancy is inflammatory and can raise the level
🚩 Calprotectin is sensitive but NOT specific — it is also raised by NSAIDs, GI infection, coeliac disease and colorectal cancer, so a high value does not by itself diagnose IBD. Critically, it is a triage tool for patients WITHOUT alarm features only: weight loss, PR bleeding, anaemia (iron deficiency), age >50, or a family history of bowel cancer/IBD mandate direct referral for colonoscopy regardless of the calprotectin result.
🎓 A normal calprotectin makes IBD unlikely and supports an IBS diagnosis, sparing the patient a colonoscopy. A raised level is non-specific and always needs endoscopic confirmation before diagnosing IBD — and remember NSAIDs falsely elevate it, so ask about them before acting on a high result.
In KNOWN IBD, calprotectin is used to→monitor disease activity, track mucosal healing (a treat-to-target endpoint), predict relapse in clinical remission, and gauge response to steroids/biologics (a falling level after induction = responder). IBD ›
Raises calprotectin apart from IBD→NSAIDs, PPIs, GI infection, coeliac, diverticular disease, colorectal cancer and older age — it is sensitive but not specific, so confirm before labelling IBD. Diverticular disease › Coeliac ›
Not a cancer test — contrast FIT→FIT detects occult haemoglobin (bleeding → colorectal-cancer risk); calprotectin detects inflammation, not blood. Colorectal cancer ›
Borderline vs normal result→borderline (~50–150) → repeat in 4–6 weeks and correlate clinically; normal → supports IBS, safety-net to re-present if symptoms persist or red flags develop. IBS ›
🎓 Exam pearl. Two jobs: (1) IBS vs IBD triage in symptomatic young patients without alarm features (normal → avoid colonoscopy); (2) monitoring known IBD (activity, mucosal healing, relapse, treatment response). It is not a cancer test — that is FIT.
GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__FIT (Faecal Immun:
The Faecal Immunochemical Test (FIT) is a quantitative stool test that uses an antibody to detect human haemoglobin (globin) in faeces. It is used both in the NHS bowel cancer screening programme and, increasingly, to risk-stratify symptomatic patients in primary care so that those most likely to have colorectal cancer are prioritised for urgent colonoscopy. The result is reported in micrograms of haemoglobin per gram of faeces (µg Hb/g).

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

FIT detects occult (invisible) blood in stool. Bowel tumours and adenomas bleed intermittently, releasing haemoglobin into the lumen before any visible blood or symptoms appear.

Screening: offered to the eligible population (in England, adults aged 50–74) every 2 years to detect asymptomatic cancers and pre-malignant polyps.
Symptomatic triage: NICE recommends FIT to guide urgent suspected-cancer referral in patients with lower-GI symptoms (e.g. change in bowel habit, abdominal pain, unexplained weight loss).
Globin-specific antibody: the test binds the globin protein of human haemoglobin.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

The patient collects a single small sample of stool at home using a probe built into a collection bottle containing buffer, then returns it to the laboratory.

No dietary preparation: unlike the old guaiac test (gFOBT), FIT does not react with dietary animal blood or plant peroxidases, so no restriction of red meat, vegetables or vitamin C is required.
Single sample: one specimen is sufficient for symptomatic testing (screening historically used one sample per round).
Quantitative: an automated immunoassay measures the haemoglobin concentration, giving a numerical µg Hb/g result compared against a threshold.
3INTERPRETATION

The result is read against a defined cut-off. In symptomatic primary care the widely used threshold is ≥10 µg Hb/g.

Symptomatic patient, FIT ≥10 µg Hb/g→Refer on the urgent suspected-cancer (2-week-wait) pathway for colonoscopy
Screening FIT positive (above programme threshold)→Invite for colonoscopy to investigate the source of bleeding
FIT negative but ongoing alarm symptoms→Still refer — FIT does not exclude cancer in a high-risk presentation
Globin-specific detection→Preferentially detects lower-GI bleeding (upper-GI globin is digested in transit)
🧪FIT (immunochemical)
Antibody to human globin; quantitative; no diet prep needed
🥩gFOBT (guaiac, old)
Peroxidase reaction; reacts with dietary blood; needed restrictions
📏Threshold ≥10 µg/g
Symptomatic cut-off triggering urgent referral
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
Not a rule-out: a negative FIT reduces but does not eliminate the probability of cancer; it stratifies risk rather than excluding disease.
Intermittent bleeding: tumours bleed variably, so a single sample can miss a lesion that is not bleeding that day.
Iron-deficiency anaemia / rectal mass: strong red flags warrant referral independent of the FIT result.
Upper-GI source: because globin is digested, FIT is insensitive to bleeding from the stomach or small bowel.
🚩 A negative FIT does NOT exclude colorectal cancer. A patient with a palpable rectal or abdominal mass, unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia, or other strong red-flag features must be referred on the urgent pathway regardless of the FIT result. FIT stratifies risk — it is not a rule-out test for high-risk presentations.
🎓 FIT detects human haemoglobin, needs no dietary prep, and is quantitative. A result ≥10 µg Hb/g triggers urgent (2-week-wait) referral in symptomatic patients. It is used both for population screening and for symptomatic triage in primary care.
Two thresholds, one test→symptomatic (NICE NG12/DG56) ≥10 µg Hb/g → urgent 2-week-wait colorectal referral; screening (England, 50–74, 2-yearly) ≥120 µg Hb/g → colonoscopy. Screening uses a higher cut-off to balance detection against colonoscopy capacity in an asymptomatic population. Bowel screening ›
Choosing the stool test→FIT for bleeding / colorectal-cancer risk (→ colorectal referral); faecal calprotectin for mucosal inflammation (IBD vs IBS). Pick by whether the concern is malignancy or inflammation.
Service role of FIT→ranks the 2-week-wait queue and spares lower-risk symptomatic patients an unnecessary colonoscopy — but a negative FIT with red flags (rectal mass, iron-deficiency anaemia) still warrants referral. Iron-deficiency anaemia ›
🎓 Exam pearl. One test, two thresholds: 10 (symptomatic 2WW) vs 120 (screening). A negative FIT never excludes cancer — ongoing red flags override the result and mandate referral. Colorectal cancer ›
GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__C. difficile Toxi:
Two-step Clostridioides difficile testing is a laboratory algorithm performed on unformed (diarrhoeal) stool to diagnose C. difficile infection (CDI). It combines a highly sensitive screen for glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH) — an enzyme made by all C. difficile, toxigenic or not — with a specific test for toxin A/B, which is the mediator of clinical disease. The two results together separate true infection from mere colonisation.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Test any patient with new-onset diarrhoea (≥ 3 unformed stools in 24 h) in the setting of risk factors, particularly recent antibiotics, PPIs, advanced age, or a hospital/care-home stay. The classic precipitating antibiotics are worth memorising.

💊Clindamycin
Classic historical trigger
💊Cephalosporins
Broad-spectrum, high risk
💊Co-amoxiclav
Common ward culprit
💊Quinolones
e.g. ciprofloxacin
GDH is an abundant enzyme expressed by all strains of C. difficile, so it is a sensitive but non-specific SCREEN for the organism's presence.
Toxin A/B is produced only by toxigenic strains and directly causes colitis, so detecting it CONFIRMS active disease rather than carriage.
Antibiotics and PPIs disrupt the protective colonic flora, allowing toxigenic C. difficile to overgrow and release toxin.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

Only liquid or unformed stool is accepted — the sample must take the shape of its container. Testing proceeds in stages so that laboratory resources and specific assays are used efficiently.

Step 1 — Screen: a GDH enzyme immunoassay (often combined with a toxin EIA on the same cartridge) is run first because it is fast and sensitive.
Step 2 — Confirm: if GDH is positive, a specific toxin A/B EIA is performed; a nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT/PCR) for the toxin gene can be used to resolve discrepant results.
A single fresh specimen is usually sufficient; there is no need to send multiple daily samples routinely.
3INTERPRETATION

Read the two results as a pair, always alongside the clinical picture.

GDH positive + Toxin positive→C. difficile infection — treat
GDH positive + Toxin negative→Potential carrier or early/low-toxin disease — interpret clinically, PCR may clarify
GDH negative→C. difficile infection unlikely — look for another cause
Management of confirmed CDI: stop the precipitating antibiotic where possible, isolate the patient, and start oral vancomycin first-line (or fidaxomicin).
Assess severity and watch for complications: pseudomembranous colitis and toxic megacolon.
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
Testing formed stool is invalid — a positive result then reflects colonisation, not infection, and risks over-treatment.
Do not test for cure: toxin and GDH can persist for weeks after clinical recovery, so a repeat positive does not mean treatment failure.
A GDH+/toxin− result is ambiguous and must never be read in isolation from bowel frequency and inflammatory markers.
🚩 Do NOT send formed stool and do NOT re-test to confirm cure — toxin can persist after recovery. A rising WCC, rising lactate, abdominal distension or ileus signals severe/fulminant colitis (toxic megacolon) and needs urgent senior and surgical review.
🎓 GDH screens, toxin confirms. GDH+/toxin− means carrier or needs PCR; GDH− effectively excludes CDI. Only test diarrhoeal stool, and first-line treatment is oral vancomycin.
GI PHYSIOLOGY & STOOL__Faecal Elastase (:
Faecal elastase-1 is a simple, non-invasive stool test used to screen for pancreatic exocrine insufficiency (PEI) — the failure of the pancreas to secrete enough digestive enzymes, leading to fat malabsorption. A low value points to conditions such as chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis or pancreatic cancer/resection, typically presenting with steatorrhoea, weight loss and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency.

1Indication & principle
Used to investigate suspected PEI in patients with steatorrhoea (pale, greasy, offensive, hard-to-flush stools), unexplained weight loss, bloating and signs of fat-soluble vitamin (A, D, E, K) deficiency.
Common underlying causes: chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis, pancreatic cancer and pancreatic resection.
Principle: elastase-1 is a pancreatic enzyme that is stable through gut transit and not degraded, so its concentration in a single stool sample reflects pancreatic exocrine output.
The assay is human-specific, so porcine-derived pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT) does not cross-react and does not need to be stopped before testing.
2How it is performed
A single random stool sample is collected and sent to the lab — no timed collection, dietary loading or fasting is required.
Elastase-1 concentration is measured by ELISA and reported in micrograms per gram of stool.
Ideally test a formed stool; enzyme supplements can be continued throughout.
3Interpretation
Faecal elastase >200 µg/g→Normal exocrine function
100–200 µg/g→Mild–moderate exocrine insufficiency
<100 µg/g→Severe pancreatic exocrine insufficiency
Low elastase + steatorrhoea→Start PERT (Creon) with meals + fat-soluble vitamin (A, D, E, K) replacement
🧪Elastase-1
Pancreatic enzyme; stable marker of exocrine output
💊Creon (PERT)
Enzyme replacement taken with every meal/snack
🩸Vitamins A D E K
Fat-soluble vitamins to replace in PEI
4Pitfalls & limitations
A watery/loose stool dilutes the sample and can give a falsely low result — test a formed stool where possible.
A normal faecal elastase does not fully exclude mild insufficiency.
The test detects insufficiency but does not identify the cause, so image the pancreas (CT/MRI) to look for chronic pancreatitis or malignancy.
🚩 Beware a falsely low value from a watery/loose stool — ideally test a formed stool. A normal result does not exclude mild insufficiency, and the test does not reveal the underlying cause: always image the pancreas (CT/MRI) to exclude chronic pancreatitis or malignancy.
🎓 Faecal elastase <100 µg/g = severe pancreatic exocrine insufficiency. It is measured on a single stool sample, and enzyme supplements need NOT be stopped (the assay is human-specific). Treat with Creon and fat-soluble vitamins.
